questions.question: What is Gin and how does it differ from Go's standard net/http?
questions.title: Introduction To Gin
questions.direct_answer: A high-performance HTTP web framework: routing with path params (c.Params), middleware chains, JSON binding/validation, and context (gin.Context) — built ON net/http, not replacing it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: A high-performance HTTP web framework: routing with path params (c.Params), middleware chains, JSON binding/validation, and context (gin.Context) — built ON net/http, not replacing it.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Gin sits on net/http and adds the framework ergonomics:

```go
r := gin.Default()  // logger + recovery middleware
r.GET("/users/:id", func(c *gin.Context) {
    id := c.Param("id")                    // path parameter
    c.JSON(200, gin.H{"id": id, "name": "Al"})  // JSON response
})
r.POST("/users", func(c *gin.Context) {
    var req CreateUserReq
    c.BindJSON(&req)  // decode + validation
    c.JSON(201, gin.H{"created": true})
})
r.Run(":8080")
```

What it adds over ServeMux + handlers:
1. Path params built-in (:id — c.Param("id"), no PathValue call — pre-1.22 this was the killer feature; 1.22's mux narrowed the gap)
2. Middleware as first-class chains (r.Use(...), group-scoped: r.Group("/api").Use(auth))
3. JSON binding with validation (c.BindJSON + binding:"required" tags)
4. The gin.Context — one object for params, JSON response, errors, abort (the framework's universal currency)
5. Route groups (r.Group("/api/v1") — versioned prefixes with shared middleware)

What it ISN'T: a different HTTP engine — it uses net/http's Server underneath (r.Run calls http.ListenAndServe with its own handler). The routing is a replacement for ServeMux; the transport is still the standard library's.

The trade: framework convenience + ecosystem (Gin middleware libraries) vs stdlib zero-dependency + Go 1.22's native routing. Both are defensible; the handler-signature difference (gin.Context vs (w, r)) is the commitment.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    G[gin.Engine] --> M[routing radix tree]
    G --> C[gin.Context: params, JSON, errors]
    G --> MW[r.Use middleware]
    G --> STD[underneath: net/http Server]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The performance story, which interviewers ask about: Gin's claims (~40x faster routing than some frameworks) rest on its radix-tree path matcher — a prefix tree over path segments, O(path-length) matching regardless of route count. Pre-1.22, ServeMux was a map+prefix walk (O(1) for exact, O(pattern-count) for subtrees); 1.22's rewrite made ServeMux competitive for realistic route counts. For any given service, the routing choice is now a DX decision, not a performance one — handler execution dominates.

gin.Context, one layer down: it wraps the http.Request and http.ResponseWriter (it IS an http.Handler internally — the engine adapts gin handlers to the standard interface). The conveniences (c.Param, c.JSON, c.Set/c.Get for per-request values, c.Error for error accumulation) are the API surface that makes handlers terse — and the coupling: a Gin handler can't serve in a non-Gin router without adaptation (unlike a plain http.HandlerFunc, which is universal).

The stdlib-vs-framework architecture conversation that closes the question: stdlib + chi gives the middleware ergonomics with the standard handler signature (portable handlers, zero framework lock-in); Gin gives the fastest path from zero to a working CRUD API with binding/validation built in. The choice is 'what am I optimizing for' — and the honest answer names both: Gin for velocity, stdlib+chi for portability, and neither is wrong.
